title: Kickin' It Old Skool
full_review:
"Kickin' It Old Skool" (Yari) uses the tired old plot device of the hero who wakes up to a new world after a number of years in a coma.

This insipid reworking begins in 1986. Five-year-old Justin (Alexander Calvert) is a break-dancing master. During a school dance contest, Justin attempts a complicated move, lands on his head and is knocked out.

Twenty years later, Justin (now played by the insufferable Jamie Kennedy) wakes up, a child in an adult body, unaware that anything has changed. Kennedy mugs like Jerry Lewis in the 1960s, managing to give offense to every minority group in the process.

Predictable time-warp confusions ensue, such as the revelation that porn can now be seen at home on the Internet. One comes perilously close to tastelessness when Justin (thinking he's still a child) innocently asks a young boy in a toy store to come home with him to play. (A nearby security guard assumes he's a predator.)

The Smurf-size plot revolves around Justin getting together his dance mates from childhood -- when they were known as "The Funky Fresh Boys" -- and entering a dance competition. All of them have their own childlike reasons for wanting to win the $100,000 first prize. As for Justin, he hopes to help his parents, who fail to comprehend that he's all grown up now.

Then there is beautiful Jen (Maria Menounos), Justin's first true love. She happens to be engaged to his old nemesis, Kip (Michael Rosenbaum, Lex Luthor on "Smallville"). Kip is running the MTV-style contest, and as he is the bad guy, he brings in a team of break-dance ringers.

Endless 1980s references abound. Emmanuel Lewis shows up at a club. David Hasselhoff loans Justin a car much like KITT from his old TV series, "Knight Rider." This movie is "Back to the Future" in reverse.

Harv Glazer directs with an inconsistent tone, and goes from sentimental to silly slapstick in a flash. All the actors mug shamelessly save for Rosenbaum, whose dry wit adds a measure of class.

The film contains suggestive dancing, drinking, brief male rear nudity, a comic scene of cross-dressing, numerous scatological gags, a brief reference to Internet pornography, one use of the f-word, frequent crude and crass language, an instance of profanity and mild sexual banter. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
